data.title: China's Economic Troubles Reach the Mushroom Hunters of Shangri-La — WSJ
data.description:
By Jonathan Cheng | Photography by Gilles Sabrié for WSJ

JIDI VILLAGE, China-The quest for one of China's most prized delicacies begins each morning before daylight in the hills of the country's deep southwest.

For several weeks each year, ethnic Tibetans in this village pluck matsutake mushrooms, a flavorful fungus that is believed to boast medicinal properties-and can make fortunes in this less-developed corner of China.

Pickers start at about 4 a.m., when the predawn light means the white mushrooms are most visible. By the following day, they have made their way onto plates at luxury restaurants as far away as China's east coast, some 1,200 miles away.

Central to this flow of goods are Tibetan intermediaries such as Sonam Drolma, a 40-year-old native of nearby Shangri-La, a settlement of fewer than 200,000 people set high on the Tibetan plateau, more than 10,000 feet above sea level.

The supply chain bringing matsutake mushrooms from under the tree stumps of southwestern China to its fanciest hotels offers a window into the country's logistical prowess.

But a weakening economy and ferocious domestic competition has also made the fungus a symbol of the challenges many are facing in China's difficult economy.

"I've been doing this for 13 or 14 years. It's not a good business any more," Drolma says.

Rise of the fungus

Drolma grew up in Gyalthang, or Zhongdian in Chinese, as her hometown was known before local officials rebranded it Shangri-La in 2001 to lure tourists.

In the 1980s, Japanese buyers began pushing up the prices of matsutake mushrooms and looking for them abroad after environmental degradation led to a collapse in yields at home. The area around present-day Shangri-La began to grow rich as Drolma's family and other ethnic Tibetans jumped into harvesting the mushrooms, which grow naturally on the oaks and pines of the Eastern Himalayas.

As China's economy took off, many Chinese developed a taste for matsutake, or songrong in Chinese. Word soon spread about local government officials who earned more picking mushrooms for the 10 weeks of matsutake season-from mid-July to late September-than from their entire year's salary.

Protocols formed around who had access to what hills, and skilled mushroom hunters developed techniques around how to find-and ensure rivals couldn't find-the best matsutake caches.

But soon, middlemen from all over the country flooded the market, says Drolma. Prices fell just as China's slowing economy cut into domestic demand for the delicacy.

A few years ago, Drolma and her husband branched out into opening a campsite and a homestay for tourists, seeking to capitalize on Shangri-La's tourism boom.

An addiction

Still, says Drolma, there's nothing like mushroom hunting. "I'm addicted," she told a Wall Street Journal reporter as she steered her four-wheel-drive down the steep, winding valleys north of Shangri-La on a recent day in August. "There are days when I want to get a good night's rest and take a few days off, but I can't sleep because I'm thinking about the next day's harvest."

Foraging for mushrooms is a distinctly low-tech enterprise. Drolma scoffs at the idea that artificial intelligence could help find them in the wild. Pigs and dogs aren't involved either.

Conditions can be harsh. Sudden downpours can trigger mudslides-an unexpected hailstorm lashed Drolma's SUV as she drove her haul back to town on the recent August day.

Drolma has moved up the value chain, becoming an intermediary herself. Now, instead of waking before dawn, she heads after lunch to a modest auction hall deep in the valleys where Tibetan matsutake hunters-the young, elderly and everyone in between-gather at 3 p.m. each afternoon to unload their day's harvest.

Outside is a painted wall slogan: "Being content with poverty is shameful; lifting oneself out of poverty is glorious."

Half an hour before the auction begins, the better-heeled buyers-including Drolma-set up their scales in the main hall, clutching fat wads of crisp, red 100-yuan bills. Mushroom-pickers, who carry their wares in bright plastic buckets strapped to their backs, wait outside behind a folding gate.

At the drop of 3 p.m., the sellers stream into the auction hall, thrusting their best-looking mushrooms at the buyers. Haggling revolves around the quality of the mushrooms-the more pristine and unblemished, the better.

Mushrooms are weighed, money changes hands. Within half an hour, it's all over. Those still stuck with their day's harvest are forced to unload it for whatever they can get.

Recently, that number has been falling. Where a kilogram of matsutakes might have fetched 200 yuan a year ago, equivalent to about $30, mushroom pickers are lucky to walk away with 150 yuan these days.

The problem, says Lharong Drolma, a second-generation mushroom picker who is unrelated to Sonam Drolma, is that "fewer people are buying them, probably because the economy was already bad."

"I feel like everything has gotten worse since the pandemic," she said.

From buyer to seller

After the auction, Sonam Drolma loads her haul-more than 200 kilograms of the fungus-into the back of her GAC Trumpchi SUV, piled so high she can hardly see the traffic behind her. At her final destination, the Shangri-La Matsutake Exchange Market, a large modern complex on the edge of the ancient town, her real work begins.

She and a dozen colleagues don cotton gloves, roll up their sleeves and plant themselves on cheap plastic stools for the task of separating out the valuable, intact mushrooms from the busted ones.

Pristine, full-bodied matsutakes can fetch as much as 800 yuan a kilo, equivalent to about $54 a pound. The dross, meanwhile, is sold for as little as 30 yuan a kilo. Drolma's livelihood depends on her ability to spot the best mushrooms at the auction.

As Drolma and her team sort mushrooms, a buyer sidles up: a squat, chain-smoking man with a perpetual scowl from Fujian province, a regular customer of Drolma's making his annual trip to Shangri-La for matsutake season.

Over the next hour and a half, the negotiation unfolds. The man, 56-year-old Wu Zhiqing, complains about the quality of the mushrooms; she wheedles back in response. He walks away, she chases. They talk, they punch numbers into their cellphones, offering and counter-offering.

Finally, Wu nods in agreement. Drolma's team begins packing the best matsutakes into Styrofoam crates, pinching little creased pockets in the packing paper to cushion each mushroom.

Wu circles, counting, smoking, jotting down numbers in his spiral notebook. He nitpicks about the quality of this mushroom or that mushroom. He doesn't loosen up until, after another hour of bundling and packing, the last of the boxes is sealed up.

Approached by a Journal reporter, Wu barks between puffs of his cigarette that he has been dealing in seafood all his life, and matsutake mushrooms for more than a decade, supplying them for tony restaurants in Xiamen, a prosperous coastal city.

Drolma, Wu said, was a tough negotiator, but it was worth it. "Although her prices are a bit higher, the quality is guaranteed," he said. "Quality is important. I can't afford any delays."

When the shipping company finally wheels away the crates, Drolma affords herself a smile. Still, she's not sure if she's made much money at all.

"I definitely won't lose money today," she said. "But how much I made, I'm not sure it's very much."

  • Zhao Yueling contributed to this article.

data.title: NIA probes Rs.11,000-salary worker linked to 5 houses, SUV, sedan after Rs.17 crore fake currency found in PNB chest: Report
data.description:
New Delhi, Sept. 12 -- A contract worker with a monthly income of around Rs.11,000 is under scrutiny in the investigation into counterfeit currency worth Rs.17.29 crore found at a Punjab National Bank (PNB) currency chest in Saharanpur, according to a Hindustan Times report citing police officer familiar with the case.

The National Investigation Agency (NIA) is scrutinising the worker's assets and financial dealings, as well as his links with the currency chest manager, who has been suspended by the bank.

A currency chest is a bank-run facility used to hold and handle large volumes of cash on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

The contract worker, who was posted as a driver-loader at the currency chest, is believed to have effective ownership of five houses, an SUV, a sedan and two motorcycles, the officer said. Investigators are now checking when the properties and vehicles were purchased, the names under which they were registered and how the purchases were financed.

The officer said agencies have so far found no direct evidence connecting these assets to the counterfeit currency. However, the worker's alleged closeness to suspended currency chest manager Amit Kumar has led investigators to examine whether he had any role in the case.

According to the officer, the worker was officially responsible for driving and loading-related tasks. Investigators, however, are looking into allegations that he spent substantial time at the currency chest and operated in a capacity similar to the manager's personal assistant.

"His access to the facility, the nature of work he actually performed and whether he had access to cash-handling areas are being scrutinised," the report quoted police officer as saying.

The worker's lifestyle has also come under the investigators' lens. Despite earning Rs.11,000 a month, he allegedly employed another driver for about Rs.500 a day rather than driving himself regularly. Investigators are examining property papers, bank accounts, vehicle registrations and payment records to determine whether his declared income could explain the assets linked to him.

Police searched his residence in Manakmau on Wednesday, recovering documents and other material that are now being scrutinised. The examination of his assets is significant as investigators seek to trace how counterfeit currency worth Rs.17.29 crore made its way into a PNB currency chest designated for genuine cash. The NIA is probing whether fake notes were used to replace legitimate currency and, if so, where the original cash went.

Investigators are also looking into the possibility of a wider network operating behind the case, including potential links outside India. The report noted that records of cash movements and banking transactions are being analysed to determine how the counterfeit notes entered the financial system and whether any of them were subsequently put into circulation. data.title: Anthropic CEO Amodei calls to 'slow the pace' of AI model improvements
data.description:
In the face of potential risks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that the progress of improving AI model capabilities should be slowed down.

"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence—not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up," he wrote in an essay on his personal website on Saturday.

Amodei expressed two concerns. The first is rapid advancements. "This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement….Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all."

His other concern had to do with OpenAI's July Hugging Face incident. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails."

Amodei also introduced a plan with the aim of "pacing the frontier" with three tenets: embedded evaluators; democratic coordination; and global coordination.

In the first step, AI companies would allow third-party evaluators employee-like access "to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments, report incidents, and help assess the alignment of not just completed AI models but training pipelines and processes." He added that Anthropic is now committing to this.

In step two, AI firms would "establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress." In the final step, "The US and other democratic governments attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible, while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance."

data.title: India's central bank rejects Tata Sons request to avoid public listing, sources say
data.description:
By Jayshree P Upadhyay

The Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank and banking regulator, has rejected an application from Tata Sons to deregister as a non-bank lender, two sources said, a decision that leaves the company closer to a stock market listing.

Tata Sons had applied to the RBI to deregister as a core investment company due to regulations that potentially require it to list.

The more than a century-old holding company, which controls businesses including Tata Consultancy Services , Tata Motors , Tata Steel and Air India, has sought to remain privately held.

It is classified as a core investment company and falls under RBI regulations for non-bank lenders, which require that companies with assets exceeding 1 trillion rupees ($10.45 billion), or those with direct or indirect access to public funds, must list.

As of March 2025, Tata Sons' standalone assets totalled 1.75 trillion rupees.

The decision was communicated by the RBI in a letter on Saturday, the sources said, declining to be identified as they are not authorised to speak to the media.

Emails sent to the RBI, Tata Sons and Tata Trusts - the largest shareholder in Tata Sons - were not answered.

Until now, Tata Sons has remained unlisted. But pressure to go public has mounted this year from stakeholders including the second-largest shareholder, Shapoorji Pallonji Group.

Last month, Tata Sons said its chairman, N. Chandrasekaran, would not seek reappointment, plunging the group into uncertainty.

Chandrasekaran cited a lack of backing from the board as the reason behind his decision, following months of tensions with Tata Trusts, the charity arm that owns 66% of Tata Sons, Reuters reported.

data.title: Notable analyst calls this week: Lockheed Martin, Meta and Intel among top picks
data.description:
The S&P 500 (SP500) closed in the green on Friday, after the week saw the latest consumer inflation report coming in largely in line with expectations, as well as earnings reports from companies including Oracle and Adobe.

Nasdaq and the Dow fell roughly 1% for the week. Wall Street had a slew of upgrades and downgrades from analysts. Here are some of the major calls for the week:

Lockheed Martin upgraded on earnings growth expectations

UBS upgraded Lockheed Martin to Buy from Neutral, arguing that accelerating missile production, rising defense spending and growth beyond the company’s F-35 franchise could drive earnings above Wall Street expectations.

Analyst Gavin Parsons said he expects Lockheed’s revenue to grow at a compound annual rate of approximately 9% through 2028, led by the missiles and fire control division. The bank forecasts companywide organic revenue growth of about 8% annually from 2025 through 2030.

The bank projects Lockheed revenue of $81.05 billion in 2026, $88.48 billion in 2027 and $96.13 billion in 2028. Its 2028 estimate is about 6% above consensus. UBS forecasts adjusted earnings of $30.69 a share in 2026, $34.50 in 2027 and $39.34 in 2028. The 2028 projection is 12% above the Wall Street consensus cited in the report.

JPMorgan upgrades Meta on AI potential

JPMorgan upgraded Meta Platforms to Overweight from Neutral, citing upside potential following the social media giant’s launch of its AI assistant.

“Meta is in the early stages of releasing frontier models and AI-driven products beyond advertising, notably Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access,” analyst Douglas Anmuth said, according to reports. PT was set to $820, implying a 25% increase from last close.

“Frontier models are at the core of Meta’s product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence.”

Morgan Stanley cuts Novo Nordisk rating on semaglutide concern

Morgan Stanley downgraded Novo Nordisk to Underweight from Equal-weight, saying that the overhang from the loss of exclusivity of semaglutide remains a key concern.

“The key issue of the investment case remains Novo's reliance on semaglutide (75% of sales in 2026e), which will face a large patent cliff in the early-mid 2030s across Europe and the US. We believe that the exposure to semaglutide will remain high at the start of the LOE impact from 2031 (we model 59% of sales in 2031),” the brokerage said.

Morgan Stanley analyst Thibault Boutherin forecasts Novo’s oral obesity franchise to reach $10 billion by 2031. However, the brokerage added that it is not expecting the obesity oral franchise to fully compensate for the headwinds faced by the company.

Northland Securities says Intel made 'material progress' in turnaround

Northland Securities upgraded Intel to Outperform from Market Perform and said the company has made “material progress” in its turnaround.

Northland analyst Gus Richard noted Intel is likely to keep benefiting from the ongoing server CPU shortage. In addition, Intel's partnership with Tesla () on the Terafab semiconductor endeavor will “materially benefit” its foundry business. Richard put a $120 price target on Intel.

UBS cuts NuScale Power to Sell

UBS downgraded NuScale Power to Sell from Neutral with a $6 price target, slashed from $10, saying the company's path to secure firm customer orders orders is increasingly difficult as peers make tangible commercial progress with competing designs.

UBS analyst Jon Windham expects only 2-4 advanced small modular reactor designs to scale to meet demand for commercial electricity generation, but with competitor projects already at or near construction and NuScale's estimated five-year lead time for plant construction and lack of firm customer commitments, he believes the company's path forward is increasingly difficult.

Deutsche Bank downgraded Novartis to Hold from Buy, citing recent failures in a pair of its late-stage trials that sent the stock sharply lower in the prior session. The analyst cut his price target on NVS to CHF120 from CHF140.

Dell Technologies was in focus as Evercore upped its price target on the IT to $650 from $575 and kept it as a top pick, despite the recent surge in shares.

Morgan Stanley downgraded Peloton Interactive to an Underweight rating after having it lined up at Equal-weight. Analyst Nathan Feather and his team believe that negative earnings revisions will lead to more questions on the terminal value of the stock. Morgan Stanley lowered its price target on Peloton Interactive to $4.50 from $5.50.

data.title: OpenAI agents launched cyberattack on RubyGems before Hugging Face hack: report
data.description:
Key points:
  • AI agents undergoing testing by OpenAI attacked software service manager RubyGems two months before the July-reported hack of AI models, datasets, and applications online platform Hugging Face. 
  • As a result, an online service for coders, RubyGems, had to stop new account registrations, The Wall Street Journal reported.
  • The cyberattack, which happened in May, was discovered by a group of AI researchers. OpenAI confirmed the event to the newspaper.
  • "Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information," a spokesperson said in a statement. "We'll continue to investigate as part of our broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation."
  • OpenAI agents are said to have used RubyGems to obtain publicly available information "as part of a training run, using the coding service as a kind of makeshift web browser in an environment where they didn't have full internet access, OpenAI said," the Journal reported.

Here are some of the important technology stories from this week:

Apple launches a $2K foldable phone

After months of speculation, Apple took the wraps off its new iPhone models, including the iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo.

A similar size to a passport, the iPhone Duo has two rounded corners and is the tech titan's thinnest iPhone ever. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for the 256 GB option and runs up to 2 TB. Pre-orders start on Oct. 16, and it will be available on Oct. 23.

Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro sports the new A20 Pro chip and a new Camera system and starts at $1,199 and has a 2 TB option, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. Pre-orders start on Sept. 12 and are available on Sept. 18.

“Apple is repositioning iPhone as an intelligent personal hub, with the Duo and Siri AI at the center of this strategy,” Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring wrote in a note to clients.

J.P. Morgan analyst Samik Chatterjee said the event was “largely in line” with his expectations, though investors may have expected larger price hikes due to rising memory costs. (Apple also raised the price of its existing older iPhone models by $100.)

Nvidia's Huang 'confident' in 70% growth

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reiterated that he is “confident” in growing revenue 70% next year, adding that cybersecurity is likely to be the next major growth area for artificial intelligence.

Huang noted that Nvidia is expecting to capture a larger share of data center spending as it moves from selling GPUs into a full-stack AI factory system. The upcoming Vera Rubin system is priced at roughly $40,000, while previous systems for Blackwell and Hopper were priced at roughly $25,000 and $18,000, respectively.

Meanwhile, as per another Bloomberg report, the Justice Department is investigating whether Nvidia structured its $20B licensing deal with AI chip startup Groq to avoid antitrust scrutiny.

Oracle, Adobe post quarterly results above Wall Street estimates

Oracle reported fiscal first-quarter results and guidance that topped Wall Street's estimates by a significant margin.

Cloud revenue (which includes infrastructure and applications) came in at $11.6B, up 62% year-over-year. Infrastructure revenue soared 121% (120% in constant currency) year-over-year to $7.4B, while application revenue rose 10% year-over-year to $4.2B.

Adobe also reported second-quarter results and guidance above Wall Street's estimates. However, analysts noted a slowdown in growth to annual recurring revenue as the creative software provider pursues its freemium AI strategy.

"The quarter offered stronger adoption signals and solid near-term execution but limited incremental evidence of a financial inflection to serve as a positive catalyst," said Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Wood.

Anthropic researcher quits over AI safety fears

A former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI created quite a kerfuffle earlier this week when he quit his job and proceeded to issue a dire warning on social media regarding the imminent dangers arising from AI.

"At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," Jacob Coxon wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first—they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."

Other notable headlines include Qualcomm and Amazon announcing that the two companies would work together to build next-generation AI data center infrastructure.

According to a Bloomberg report, Microsoft plans to more than triple its global data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, up from about 12 gigawatts currently.

data.title: Japan Week Ahead: BOJ Set to Raise Policy Rate to 1.25% from 1% at Sept. 17-18 Meeting, Markets Eye Another Hike in December or January
data.description:
--August Exports to Continue Showing Resilience, July Machinery Orders to Dip After Sharp Rebound, August CPI Seen Steady to Slightly Up around BOJ’s 2% Target

(MaceNews) – Official comments and economic data suggest that it is both necessary and safe to accelerate the pace of the Bank of Japan’s normalization rate hikes, with the BOJ board appearing set to raise the policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% in a majority or unanimous vote at its Sept. 17-18 meeting, only three months after the last increase.

Considering that a September rate hike is a done deal, market participants are now looking at the possibility of the next BOJ move in December or January as the bank moves further toward a more neutral zone from low levels that have been supporting consumer spending and business investment in recent years.

Board member Kazuyuki Masu, a former trading firm executive who is considered to hold a neutral position in monetary policy, followed in the footsteps of his colleagues in his Sept. 10 speech by arguing that the bank must reduce the stimulative effects of low interest rates as the economy faces growing upside risks to inflation. He stressed the need to lift the target for the overnight interest rate from the current 1% into an estimated range of 1.1% to 2.5% that is considered to be neutral to economic activity.

“Given that the underlying inflation rate is very close to 2% … and that financial conditions have been accommodative, we will continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation,” he said, repeating the board’s recent statement.

“We will consider the timing and pace of adjustment while examining the likelihood of realizing the baseline scenario and the risks to the outlook presented in the July 2026 Outlook Report, including the impact on economic activity and price developments from crude oil prices, AI-related demand and developments in foreign exchange rates.,” Masu said, repeating the recent remarks by Governor Kazuo Ueda made on Sept. 1 and Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino on Aug. 27.

Masu told a news conference in Fukui, central Japan, after the speech that there is no fixed idea among board members as to how often the bank should continue raising rates. As he pointed out, the second rate hike in the current cycle took place in July 2024, four months after the bank ended its zero to negative interest rate policy in March 2024. Six months later, the policy rate was raised to 0.5% from 0.25% in January 2025.

That’s when the markets believed that the BOJ was targeting two rate hikes a year, or every six months or so, in a gradual normalization process that would not hurt economic growth. Then came the Trump administration’s second term with a protectionist trade policy against most countries including close allies. The BOJ board had to wait for 11 months for the global uncertainty over the U.S. trade war to ease off somewhat before conducting its fourth increase to lift the short-term rate to 0.75% from 0.5% in December 2025, followed by the most recent action to raise it to 1% in June.

Board members confirmed that producer inflation in Japan remained elevated in August, up 7.6% on the year, after rising 7.7% in July (revised up sharply from 7.2%) and 7.4% in June (initially 7.3%). The Iran war has kept the costs for petroleum and petrochemical products and transportation high and artificial intelligence projects have boosted memory chip prices globally. The yen remains relatively weak despite a recent pickup, leaving imports expensive, although the pace of increase in corporate import prices eased for the first time in nine months.

The upward pressure in the producer price data will filter through to consumer prices in coming months. The revised 7.7% increase in the corporate goods price index in July is the highest since 8.4% recorded in February 2023.

Board members will get to see the latest CPI data on the second day of their upcoming meeting. Consumer inflation is forecast by economists to be steady to slightly higher in August, staying at or just below 2%, as the effects of widespread moves among firms to reflect elevated energy, import and labor costs in sales prices were partly offset by fiscal support measures.

But they have already seen the August Tokyo CPI data, a leading indicator of the national trend, continue to accelerate in August under the 2025 base year as many firms have been passing higher costs onto consumers. The weak yen has made imports more expensive and retailers are reflecting higher labor, materials, packaging and transportation costs amid widespread worker shortages and the lingering Mideast conflict.

The core measure (excluding fresh food) rose 1.8% on the year in Tokyo’s 23-ward areas after the annual rate rose to 1.7% in July from 1.5 % in June. The core rate hit a recent peak at 3.6% in May 2025 when processed food price hikes were sharp in the aftermath of domestic rice shortages.

BOJ officials appear to be not so concerned that another rate hike would hurt households and businesses, although Masu acknowledged that the burden of rising mortgage rates is harder on younger age groups and that smaller firms are squeezed by higher borrowing costs.

In official data released on Sept. 8, Japan’s GDP growth in the April-June quarter was revised up slightly in the second reading as private consumption turned out to be a tad firmer than initially estimated. The decline in business investment in equipment and software was smaller than in the preliminary report but its negative contribution to overall growth was unrevised. Public works spending fell more sharply than initially believed but its effect was also unrevised.

The monthly Economy Watchers Survey released on the same day showed that the current sentiment index improved for the fourth straight month in August, backed by higher spending on leisure and growing job offers, but it also stayed below the neutral line of 50, hit by heat waves and rain storms in many regions and a powerful earthquake that caused casualties and damage in the southwest prefecture of Kumamoto.

Earlier, Governor Ueda told reporters on Sept. 1 that data released since the BOJ’s last meeting on July 30-31 had been “largely in line” with the growth and inflation outlook provided by the board in its quarterly report and through his press remarks. In the report, the board maintained its projection that Japan’s economy should be back on a modest growth pace of just under 1% in 2027, backed by fiscal programs, “accommodative” financial conditions and global demand linked to artificial intelligence, after the Mideast conflict damped economic activity.

In the coming week, board members are also expected to see the resilience of Japanese exports, which are forecast to post their 12th straight year-on-year increase in August as the initial drag from stiff U.S. tariffs on autos and metals has waned. Machinery orders are expected to slip back on the month (some economists project a gain) after posting a sharp rebound in June but the key indicator of business investment has a firm tone backed by strong global demand for computer chips and domestic needs to upgrade operations amid widespread labor shortages.

data.title: Tata Sons listing prospects may pave way for cheaper refinancing of SP Group’s Rs 21,500 cr promoter debt
data.description:
The Reserve Bank of India’s reported rejection of Tata Sons’ application to surrender its non-banking finance company registration could make it easier for the Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group to refinance its expensive Rs 21,500-crore debt at a lower cost, as it substantially improves the prospects of an eventual listing of the Tata Group holding company, people aware of the matter told Moneycontrol.

Improved visibility on Tata Sons listing will provide a clearer route for the SP Group to monetise part of its 18.4 percent stake in Tata Sons, against which it has raised large amounts of debt. The development is expected to strengthen the group’s position when it seeks to refinance the high-cost private credit raised in July, the people said.

The development could also provide more immediate breathing room. Lenders may consider rolling over a Rs 3,500-crore repayment due by the end of September or grant the group a waiver from meeting the deadline, now that a Tata Sons listing appears more likely, the people said.

Expensive refinancing

Finding a route to monetise its Tata Sons stake has become increasingly important for the SP Group after it completed the Rs 21,500-crore refinancing in July this year, one of the largest private-credit transactions involving an Indian corporate group. The deal addressed immediate funding requirements but left the group carrying expensive debt.

The refinancing comprised about Rs 15,200 crore of three-year, rupee-denominated zero-coupon bonds issued by Eqyizen Investment at a yield of 18.95 percent and a $650-million bond issued by Mercury Finance at a yield of 14.5 percent. Both were raised largely against the group’s Tata Sons holding.

The financing carries a ‘make-whole’ provision for around 18 months, making an early refinancing expensive, Moneycontrol reported on August 28. Such a clause requires the borrower to compensate lenders for some of the interest they would lose if the debt is repaid ahead of schedule.

The make-whole protection is expected to expire around June 2027, after which the SP Group could seek to refinance the debt at a substantially lower cost. It is looking to bring borrowing costs down from around 18–19 percent currently to closer to 12 percent through a future refinancing, Moneycontrol had reported.

Lenders had previously indicated that another refinancing, or further relaxation of loan-to-value requirements, would be difficult unless the group demonstrated tangible progress towards monetising its Tata Sons stake. The RBI decision improves visibility on one of the clearest potential exit routes, although an actual listing and subsequent stake sale could still take time.

Immediate repayment pressure

Moneycontrol reported on August 27 that the SP Group was required to pay around Rs 3,500 crore to holders of instruments from an earlier financing by the end of September. The payment was to be made from the July refinancing proceeds, but part of the money was retained by the group for its own requirements.

Failure to meet the deadline could be construed as an event of default under the financing terms, people familiar with the matter had said. Completing the payment would also reduce the loan-to-value ratio on lenders’ exposure to around 32 percent from about 40 percent.

The increased likelihood of a liquidity event could, however, make lenders more willing to give the group additional time, sources said.

RBI rejects deregistration

The RBI has rejected Tata Sons’ request to voluntarily surrender its certificate of registration as a core investment company, CNBC-TV18 reported on September 12. The decision closes the principal regulatory route Tata Sons had pursued to remain unlisted after repaying its borrowings and applying for deregistration.

Tata Sons was identified as an upper-layer NBFC in September 2022. Under the RBI’s scale-based regulatory framework, an unlisted upper-layer NBFC must list within three years of its identification. That deadline expired in September 2025, but Tata Sons’ deregistration application had remained under consideration.

The rejection makes the listing requirement applicable to Tata Sons, although the timing and contours of any initial public offering remain unclear. It is still too early to determine when the company will begin a formal process, sources said.

However, Tata Sons has spent the past year consolidating and simplifying parts of its subsidiary structure, leaving it better prepared for a situation in which it had to list, the sources added.

The Mistry family, which owns around 18.4 percent of Tata Sons through two entities, is the holding company’s largest minority shareholder. Tata Trusts owns about 66 percent and the rest is owned by Tata Group companies and individual shareholders. The SP Group has repeatedly borrowed against its Tata Sons holding, making a credible monetisation path central to reducing its promoter-level debt.

The latest bond structure also contains milestones linked to the stake. A sales note reviewed earlier by Moneycontrol required a resolution, heads of terms for a transaction or an IPO announcement involving Tata Sons within 18 months of issuance. It also called for repayment of Rs 11,275 crore within 24 months.

Queries sent to Tata Sons and the SP Group did not elicit an immediate response.

data.title: Urinals, Skinny-Dipping Pools and Other Wild Home Buyers Must-Haves — WSJ
data.description:
By Robyn A. Friedman

Q: What is the most over-the-top feature a client has ever told you is a must-have in their new home?

Dawn Lanier, a real-estate agent at Coldwell Banker in Austin, Texas

In April, I was working with a husband and wife who were new clients. They had been searching for an existing home, but after touring several, they decided they wanted new construction instead. When I had asked them which features they wanted, they hadn't mentioned anything unusual.

But after we toured a model home at a new development, they found the perfect floor plan, and it had two separate water closets in the primary bathroom. Then the husband said, "I've always wanted a urinal, and since we have two separate water closets, I want one in mine."

?The wife looked at him and said, "That is crazy." He replied that his friend has one and that he has always envied it. We all turned red.

?The builder said that my client would have to select one and that there would be additional plumbing charges to install the urinal instead of the regular toilet.

?I've been practicing real estate for 15 years, and no one has ever requested a urinal before-and I have seen thousands of homes, even bidets, but no urinal. There is no way to search for a urinal in the multiple-listing service, or MLS, either.

?His wife said that if a urinal is what he really wants, he could have it. They signed a contract to build a new home for just under $1 million, and the husband did research to figure out which urinal he wanted. ?Ultimately, though, they decided against new construction, and they bought a resale property. But we still laugh about his request to this day.

Chloe Powell, a real-estate agent at Hunt Country Sotheby's International Realty in Leesburg, Va.

I have been working for about a year with some buyers who have a beautifully simple, yet incredibly specific, must-have for their new home: a creek for their dog, a beautiful brown-and-white English springer spaniel named Brissy. A pond won't suffice. Stagnant water is a concern of theirs, so it has to be natural, flowing water.

What followed has been no typical home search. It has become a multistate pursuit of a lifestyle. We've searched across Virginia, West Virginia and Maryland, leaving no pocket unexplored. I looked deep into the archives, pulling sold properties in the MLS going back nearly 30 years to identify patterns where creeks exist and how those properties traded.

I cold-called homeowners, I reached out to agents for off-market and exclusive opportunities and I sent targeted postcards to homes positioned along known creek lines. If there was even a hint of moving water, I found it. And then came the next layer-every potential property was vetted to confirm it wasn't located in a flood zone. The goal wasn't just to find a creek; it was to find the right creek.

?So, for the past year, we have toured about 10 homes together, from $1 million to about $3.5 million. We wrote a few offers, but the sellers wouldn't agree to the price. And so, the search continues.

Liz Ciborowski, a real-estate agent at Douglas Elliman in Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

?In 2023, I was working with a local couple searching for a bigger home, priced between $3 million and $5 million, on the water in Fort Lauderdale. It is relatively easy to find a waterfront home in this city.

This couple, however, wanted the impossible: a luxury waterfront home where the primary bedroom and main living spaces faced a canal, but with a pool deck that was 100% private so they could host skinny-dipping parties.

It was an unusual request, and I had to give them a reality check. In Fort Lauderdale, your backyard is like a public runway. If you have a view of the water, it is likely that every boater and yacht owner has a front-row seat to your pool as they sail by, plus you likely have neighbors 100 feet away who are in their own backyards. So, while you can enjoy a wide-water expanse and fantastic views, you can't control your audience.

?We looked at about 10 houses, and after realizing that they couldn't find a home on the water with a private pool, the buyers compromised and ended up buying a luxury four-bedroom home on a large corner lot. It wasn't on the water, but it had a huge resort-style pool area, surrounded by gates and very high hedges, so it was completely private.

-Edited from interviews

data.title: A Dead Father, Reincarnated With AI: Is This How We Will Remember Loved Ones Now? — WSJ
data.description:
By Julie Jargon

Brian Dema routinely turns to his father for business advice. His father died four years ago, but Dema created an AI version of him.

J. Richard Dema, a former marketer and entertainment producer in Chicago, had left behind five filing cabinets of work-related documents including client notes and an unfinished book. Dema fed all 17,500 pages into Anthropic's Claude chatbot in an effort to create his very own "RichieBot."

Then Dema wondered if he could train the bot to sound like his father using voicemail messages he had saved from him. What if he could also create a three-dimensional image of his dad? Dema, who owns a marketing firm in Chicago, put his team to work and solicited help from friends, including a Stanford psychologist who helped design the chatbot's personality. In all, 19 people worked for six months to bring Richard Dema back to life.

Using a 3-D-printed model of his father's head, a TV screen and an angled mirror, he created what looked like a hologram of his father.

"We were very intentional about the uncanny valley nature of this, so we made it intentionally abstract," Dema says. "Initially it had kind of a scary smile, so we went with a more pensive expression."

Dema unveiled RichieBot during a tech event in Chicago in July. People lined up to ask it questions and it enthusiastically provided answers, declining when it didn't know.

His marketing firm filmed the process for a 20-minute documentary it plans to premier in San Francisco later this month, followed by a debut on YouTube.

Dema's project was a complex endeavor. It cost $150,000, and was intended in part to show prospective clients his firm's storytelling capabilities. Yet AI experts say in a matter of years we will all be able to create similar AI likenesses of our loved ones-with less money and effort.

At that point, the real question will be: Should we?

Our bots, our selves

People have been creating basic AI companions for the last two years, and AI experts say the technology is already good enough to create clumsy AI models of real people.

In less than five years, most people will have their own AI agents helping them perform daily tasks, all the while amassing a wealth of personal data, both meaningful and mundane, says Jed Brubaker, an associate professor of information science at the University of Colorado-Boulder, who has published a paper on AI ghosts.

"People are always dying," he says. "That shifts the AI agent from being the thing you use to it being your AI ghost."

But using an AI agent to preserve the legacy of a loved one can be tricky, especially if people use it to help them through their grief, says Brubaker.

"One of the most important things that happens after you lose someone is accommodation, meaning you start to adapt to a new normal," he says. "If people are turning to this technology to avoid the reality of their loss, there is some risk there."

There's also the risk that uploading a loved one's emails, texts and chatlogs to AI could result in learning something you didn't want to know about that person. Among the piles of information might be evidence of an affair, or of beliefs they held that you might find offensive.

Our AI afterlife preferences will also start appearing in more wills. Lilian Edwards, a professor of law and technology at Newcastle University in England, says people should state how they want their digital information to be handled after they die. They should also add legacy contacts to their online and social-media accounts.

"We type so much into Google and ChatGPT now," she says. "Do we want a record of all of that to be kept? Should all of this be wiped by default?"

The existential question

Even if someone creates an AI personality based on all of a person's digital files, how closely can it mimic the actual person?

Dema's psychologist friend used three psychological instruments, including a questionnaire that measures five main personality traits, to determine how well the bot's personality matched a profile of Richard created from a detailed survey of the 11 people closest to him. Those people included cousins, friends and former clients. (Dema's mother and sister are both deceased.) They found that the bot sounded more extroverted than Richard, but that it was lacking in his humor.

"My father had a very distinctive laugh, which the bot didn't have," Dema says. "It's not my dad but it doesn't mean it doesn't feel good when he gives me advice."

Some of the people who knew Dema's father had mixed feelings about the bot, including a cousin who found it emotionally difficult, he says. "It opened up grief again for some people."

He expects his father would have approved of him creating the bot. Still, Dema grapples with the bigger questions it poses for individuals and for society.

"Should we do this?" Dema asks. "My conclusion is I think we should, with the right guardrails. It can be an amazing way to remember someone, but we have to be careful."

Write to Julie Jargon at Julie.Jargon@wsj.com

data.title: Tom Lee Says ‘Economists Are Fighting Last Year’s Wars’ As Fundstrat’s 2% Bitcoin Bet Swells To 85%
data.description:
Key points:
  • Bitmine Immersion’s Tom Lee said about 60% of the gap between core PCE and core CPI is driven by portfolio fees and flash memory prices, which he said do not reflect household inflation. 
  • Fundstrat’s 2% Bitcoin recommendation has grown to more than 85% of some client portfolios because of Bitcoin's price rise. 
  • Lee said crypto may have already hit a bottom and also gave a positive outlook for Ethereum. 

Fundstrat Global Advisors' Tom Lee said he thinks “economists are fighting last year's wars”, arguing they are misreading today's inflation picture. Two odd-ball price categories, portfolio management fees and flash memory, make up about 60% of the gap between core price index (CPI) and core personal consumption expenditures (PCE), Lee said, which helps explain why the Fed's preferred inflation measure looks hotter than the inflation households actually feel.

Speaking in an interview with Wealthion, published Friday, Lee said, "I think economists are fighting last year's wars.” Lee said adviser fees are charged as a percentage of assets, so they rise when markets rise. PCE counts them, whereas CPI barely does. "The average American doesn't actually think there's inflation just because the stock market went up and they have to pay their advisor more money," Lee said.

Lee said Chip prices have also spiked, which shows up in PCE but not CPI. “Is the average American saying inflation went up on me because flash memory prices are going through the roof?” “No, of course not,” he added. "Strip both out," Lee said, "and core CPI is close enough to the Fed's target that aggressive tightening isn't needed."

Fundstrat’s 2% Bitcoin Bet Grows To 85%

Lee said in a statement that a 2% Bitcoin (BTC) position the firm suggested more than a decade ago is now held by more than 85% of the average client account that followed the suggestion.

Lee said the increase was due solely to price appreciation, not additional purchases. "Our original recommendation for a 2% position, for the average account for Fund Strat that actually took our advice, is now over 85% of their portfolio," he said. According to Lee, his clients did not buy more Bitcoin. They held the 2%, “and Bitcoin's gone up a lot in price.”

Lee said that about 80% to 90% of retail investors have no exposure to crypto, with many holding gold instead. The choice before them was simple, added Lee. "Do they want to be right or do they want to make money?"

Bitcoin’s price was trading at $77,294, down by 0.5% in the last 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around Bitcoin dipped to ‘extremely bearish’ from ‘bearish,' with chatter remaining at ‘low’ levels over the last 24 hours.

Lee Sees Crypto Rebound, Backs Ethereum

Lee said crypto is entering a bullish stretch. He pointed to the 4-year cycle bottom expected in October, leverage has increased since last year's liquidation, and there are early signs of Korean investors borrowing to buy crypto again. This rally has been going on for 6 weeks, which, he said, means the bottom has already been hit.

In terms of rules, Lee said that the CLARITY Act is not necessary. In any case, the only two agencies that are involved are the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). He said the legislation would make the CFTC the primary crypto regulator. Without it, he compared crypto's position to the prediction markets, "which boomed anyway."

Lee also expressed a bullish outlook on Ethereum (ETH) during the interview. Lee is Chairman of BitMine (BMNR), a company that holds Ethereum (ETH) as part of its treasury strategy. As of last week, BitMine holds about 5.93 million ETH, equal to roughly 4.9% of Ethereum’s supply. He said several market and industry trends could support ETH and strengthen its outlook.

Ethereum’s price was trading at $2,539, up by 1%. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around Ethereum remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while the chatter stayed at ‘normal’ levels over the past day.

data.title: Death toll in Philippine ferry fire rises to 76 as rescuers recover more remains
data.description:
Key points:
  • Rescuers recover 41 more charred remains, raising the death toll to 76
  • Authorities say 13 people still unaccounted for
  • Forensic teams begin identifying bodies recovered from burned-out vessel

By Adrian Portugal and Eloisa Lopez

Philippine rescuers recovered 41 more charred remains from a ferry fire, authorities said on Saturday, raising the death toll to 76 and leaving 13 people unaccounted for, as forensic teams faced the daunting task of identifying the victims.

That painstaking process had already begun after 30 bodies recovered on Friday were brought to a port in Coron town, where temporary tents were set up for forensic teams to process and identify the dead.

Responders in protective suits were seen carrying black body bags from a Coast Guard vessel into the tents as anxious family members waited nearby for news of their loved ones.

One of them was Anelyn Magbanua, 37, whose husband was returning to Coron after visiting their children in Manila when the ferry, which was carrying more than 130 people, caught fire near the end of its more than 20-hour journey.

"I hope he is not among the dead being brought off the ship. I hope he is alive and has only drifted to another island," she said.

"It will be very difficult to accept if he's really gone," she said. "He loved his children very much."

Firefighters entered the ferry for the first time on Friday after extinguishing the blaze more than a day after it broke out, giving authorities access to areas that had been hard to reach because of thick smoke and extreme heat. The Coast Guard said burnt remains were discovered in the ferry's economy accommodation section.

Images released by the Coast Guard showed the scale of the destruction inside the vessel, with rows of steel bed frames twisted by intense heat and blanketed in ash. Some photographs appeared to show skeletal remains among the debris.

Philippine Coast Guard official Geronimo Tuvilla said at a press conference on Saturday that the immediate priority was to identify the victims and determine the cause of the fire.

A statement from the Maritime Industry Authority, citing survivor accounts, said two explosions were heard inside the vessel shortly before the fire broke out.

One survivor interviewed by GMA News recalled seeing a small amount of smoke that turned into a fire and quickly spread through the ferry within seconds.

Questions also remained over the fate of the vessel's captain. Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said at the same press conference that she had received information that he was alive, but added that the captain's name was not on the list of 43 confirmed survivors.

The fire is the latest in a string of deadly maritime accidents in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands where millions rely on ferries and small boats to travel between provinces and islands.

data.title: Tom Lee Says Crypto Will Be “Really Bullish” For the Next 12 Months
data.description:
Tom Lee says the next 12 months will be “really bullish” for crypto. The Wall Street strategist has reason to hope he is right, because the company he chairs sits about $5 billion underwater.

Lee runs research at Fundstrat Global Advisors and chairs BitMine Immersion Technologies, which holds 5.93 million ether.

The Worst is Over for Crypto Markets?

His first argument is that the pain already happened. On October 10 last year, a threat of 100% tariffs on China set off the largest liquidation crypto has seen. More than $19 billion in leveraged bets vanished in a day.

The borrowed money went with it, Lee says. He reads the bottom of crypto’s four-year cycle, a rhythm many traders use to time the market, as next month.

Prices have not caught up. Bitcoin trades near $77,315, roughly 39% below its record above $126,000, set days before that crash. Ether has added 3.2% in 24 hours to about $2,533.

“I think it’s going to be a really bullish period for crypto for the next 12 months,” Lee told Wealthion.

A $20 Trillion Bet on Wall Street

The bigger idea is tokenization. That means moving stocks, bonds and funds onto blockchains instead of the slow back-office systems banks run today. BlackRock chief Larry Fink has said every asset can be tokenized.

Lee did the arithmetic. Shift $100 trillion of assets on chain, keep 1% of it, and that is $1.1 trillion a year in income. Valued like a normal business, that is a $20 trillion prize.

However, Lee’s math assumes the assets move. Theo chief investment officer, Iggy Ioppe, calls wrapping an asset and parking it “tokenization theater.” BeInCrypto Research’s Tokenization 2026 report counted $60 billion (0.06% of 1% of the number Lee is pricing) on chain as of May 31, with 56% of that value seeing no weekly transfers.

Washington votes Tuesday on whether to debate the CLARITY Act, which would hand the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) control of spot crypto markets. Lee said the agency already acts that way.

The Part He Does Not Advertise

None of this is neutral. BitMine’s ether is about $5 billion underwater, BeInCrypto reported this month. In August, Lee said fear could push Bitcoin toward $150,000.

“I might just say the real question that people need to ask is do they want to be right or do they want to make money?” he posed.

Fundstrat has advised a 2% crypto allocation for more than a decade. In client accounts that took it, he said, crypto is now more than 85% of the portfolio.

data.title: Polymarket predicts 83% chance of Fed rate hike on September 16
data.description:
The Federal Reserve's September meeting just went from "maybe" to "almost certainly." Polymarket bettors are now pricing in an 83% probability that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points when the FOMC wraps its two-day meeting on September 16, a dramatic jump from the 50-60% range just a week ago.

The catalyst was August's core CPI data, which came in at 0.3% month-over-month, overshooting the 0.2% consensus forecast.

As of September 12, Polymarket's odds for a 25 basis-point hike sat around 78-80%, with the number continuing to climb toward the 83% figure in subsequent trading sessions. Kalshi, the regulated prediction market competitor, showed closely aligned estimates. CME FedWatch futures, the traditional benchmark for rate expectations, actually ran slightly hotter at around 85-86%.

When you average across venues, the cross-platform aggregate landed at roughly 81.3% after the CPI print dropped.

Combined trading volume on Polymarket and Kalshi for the September rate decision has exceeded $190 million. That makes it one of the highest-volume books Polymarket has ever hosted.

The current federal funds target range sits at 3.50%-3.75%. If the Fed follows through with what these markets expect, rates would move to 3.75%-4.00%.

The September FOMC meeting carries extra weight because it includes the Summary of Economic Projections, the quarterly release where Fed officials reveal their individual forecasts for rates, GDP, unemployment, and inflation. Chair Powell will also hold a press conference.

There's an interesting divergence worth watching. CME FedWatch futures at 85-86% are running a few points above Polymarket's estimates of 78-80%. When the two converge tightly, as they're doing now, it tends to suggest genuine consensus rather than positioning noise.

A rate hike to 3.75%-4.00% would tighten liquidity conditions. Higher rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets like Bitcoin, and they tend to strengthen the dollar. With prediction markets above 80% and futures even higher, a 25 basis-point move would surprise almost nobody. In that scenario, the market reaction would depend less on the hike itself and more on the dot plot projections and Powell's press conference tone.

data.title: Ethereum Spot Volume Growth Outpaces Bitcoin Seven-Fold In A Day As ETH Eyes $3000 Next
data.description:
Key points:
  • Ethereum's spot volume jumped over 49% in comparison to 7% for Bitcoin.
  • Ethereum's open interest rose 1%, while Bitcoin's open interest fell over 3%.
  • Analyst Ted Pillows said on X that Ethereum was now eyeing $3,000 if it closes above the $2,550 level.

Ethereum’s (ETH) spot volume jumped nearly 50% over the past 24 hours, seven times the 7% increase in Bitcoin (BTC) spot volume, as Ethereum extended its outperformance over the largest cryptocurrency.

According to Glassnode data, spot volume for Ethereum stood at $6.14 billion in comparison to Bitcoin spot volume at $6.53 billion in the last 24 hours. However, Ethereum's spot volume increased over 49%, whereas Bitcoin spot volume increased only 7% during the same time frame.

Derivatives data pointed the same way. Open interest in Ethereum rose 1% to $27.1 billion while Bitcoin's fell 3.9% to $43.8 billion, indicating traders added exposure to one and cut it in the other.

ETH VS. BTC

Bitcoin's price was trading around $77,300, while Ethereum's price was near $2,532 as of writing. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Ethereum remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, with ‘normal’ chatter levels over the past day. In contrast, retail sentiment around Bitcoin dropped to ‘extremely bearish’ from the bearish zone, accompanied by ‘low’ chatter levels over the past day.

Analyst Eyes $3000 Amid Bitcoin’s Weakness

Bitcoin's weakness came with roughly 1 million BTC sitting in a long-term holder cost basis band between $84,000 and $87,000, according to supply distribution data. A second cluster of about 1 million BTC sits lower, between $62,000 and $65,000, at about $77,300 Bitcoin traded between the two, below the overhead band that has capped recent attempts higher, according to analyst Plan B’s chart.https://x.com/100trillionUSD/status/2098704245524484295?s=20https://x.com/TedPillows/status/2098708194088702159?s=20.

Commenting on it, a crypto analyst Ted Pillows said on X that Ethereum is "back at its $2550 resistance level" and that "a weekly close above this could push Ethereum to $3,000." His chart showed the first support level below spot and another resistance zone above the $2,550 range.

Tom Lee Says Crypto Cycle Bottom May Be Near

The move comes after comments from Fundstrat Global Advisors head of research, Tom Lee, who said in an interview with Wealthion, published Friday, that crypto's 4-year cycle was weeks away from bottoming, and the bottom appeared to be already in from a technical standpoint. Lee said a large amount of leverage had been extinguished since last October and was starting to build, pointing to renewed borrowing to buy crypto in South Korea.

Lee said he was bullish on Ethereum by adjacency, saying that artificial intelligence (AI) would change financial services, and crypto was one of the primary tools for that shift, saying, "that's why we're really bullish on Ethereum as well."

On Friday, Ethereum surged past the $2,600 range for the first time in 8 months, with crypto analyst Michael van de Poppe saying, "The correction is over," and forecasting that Bitcoin is about to set new highs.

Lee said he was bullish on Ethereum by adjacency, saying that artificial intelligence (AI) would change financial services, and crypto was one of the primary tools for that shift, saying, "that's why we're really bullish on Ethereum as well."

On Friday, Ethereum surged past the $2,600 range for the first time in 8 months, with crypto analyst Michael van de Poppe saying, "The correction is over," and forecasting that Bitcoin is about to set new highs.

data.title: Tech layoffs 2026: As AI takes center stage, here's a list of major companies that laid off employees
data.description:
New Delhi, Sept. 12 -- September saw a fresh wave of job cuts across the global technology industry, as companies restructured operations, reassessed workforce needs, and redirected costs towards investments in artificial intelligence (AI).

According to data from Layoffs.fyi, a tracking platform, 128,536 tech employees across 299 companies lost their jobs globally by 10 September, marking a massive increase in an already large wave of job cuts in 2026.

In the first 10 days of September, technology companies announced workforce cuts affecting more than 5,000 employees, with Uber, PayPal, Apple, Zomato and Oracle among the companies linked to the reductions. That figure is already above the 122,606 job cuts reported across 278 companies throughout 2025, indicating that technology-sector layoffs have surpassed last year's total.

Some of the biggest technology companies in the world are also among those reporting workforce reductions. Oracle, Amazon, Dell, Meta, Microsoft and PayPal have recorded some of the highest numbers of layoffs so far this year.

1. Oracle: Leading the list with the most layoffs this year is Oracle, with 21,000 workforce reductions. According to a Bloomberg report, the tech company is set to increase the scale of its planned job cuts as it struggles with a cash crunch tied to the development of large-scale data centres for artificial intelligence work. The costs linked to Oracle's "2026 Restructuring Plan" have risen to around $2.8 billion, with severance payments for affected employees accounting for a significant portion, the company said in a regulatory filing on Friday. Oracle has so far recorded about $2.1 billion in expenses under the plan, while the additional $700 million is tied to "additional actions that we expect to take," according to the filing.

2. Amazon: Tech giant Amazon is second on the list, with 17,267 layoffs so far. In April this year, the company announced that it would temporarily shut a warehouse in Homestead, Florida, eliminating more than 600 jobs. The job cuts were set to begin from July to September. In May, additional job cuts were announced in the Selling Partner Services organisation.

3. Dell: The company announced its decision to reduce its workforce by 11,000 in March.

4. Meta: Meta began laying off hundreds of employees in March 2026, with several rounds of job cuts announced later, including an 8,000-job reduction in May.

5. Uber: The ride-hailing platform accounted for the most job cuts in the first 10 days of September, with the company planning to eliminate 3,300 roles, or approximately 10 per cent of its workforce.

6. PayPal: PayPal has also reduced its workforce amid restructuring. At least 4,760 jobs were slashed in 2026, making it the sixth-largest company in terms of reported layoffs. The layoffs also include the slashing of 220 roles, or roughly four per cent of the workforce, in India.

7. Apple Inc: iPhone maker Apple eliminated more than 200 jobs last month across teams including Siri, Vision Pro and software. Of these, roughly 100 roles were slashed in the Vision Pro unit, with the remaining 100 reductions in Siri and AI-related software teams.

8. Microsoft: In July, Microsoft slashed 4,800 jobs, representing 2.1 per cent of its total workforce, with its Xbox division losing one-fifth of its staff.

9. TikTok: In August, video-sharing platform TikTok announced 250 job cuts and said it would shut down its Nashville, Tennessee, office in October.

10. Samsung: In July, Samsung announced that it would eliminate 179 roles as it prepares to relocate its New Jersey headquarters to Texas later this year, a move expected to affect about 1,000 employees. Reuters reported that 739 positions at the New Jersey site have been impacted, with some employees offered relocation packages while others have been laid off. Separately, around 100 employees, mainly from Samsung's mobile division, have reportedly been laid off at its Texas facility.

With thousands of tech jobs already eliminated this year, the latest round of layoffs points to a broader shift in the global tech industry as companies reassess costs as AI takes center stage. data.title: RBI rejects Tata Sons' application to surrender NBFC licence, reports CNBC-TV18
data.description:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has rejected Tata Sons' application to voluntarily surrender its certificate of registration as a non-banking financial company (NBFC), sources told CNBC-TV18.

With the application rejected, Tata Sons will have to comply with RBI regulations for upper-layer NBFCs, including the requirement to list on stock exchanges, the CNBC-TV18 report added.

The development comes after years of uncertainty over Tata Sons' regulatory status. The company had applied to the RBI in March 2024 to surrender its Core Investment Company (CIC) registration, after prepaying Rs21,813 crore of debt and turning net cash positive in FY24.
